column5: name exalted above earth and heaven
column6: The commentary joins “exalt the Lord’s name” to al-aʿla; this psalm says the Lord’s name alone is exalted and his majesty is above earth and heaven, an unusually close praise formula.

column5: call on and proclaim the exalted name
column6: The commentary’s command to praise the high name is matched by Isaiah’s thanksgiving instruction to call on the Lord’s name and proclaim among the nations that it is exalted.
The commentary labels ٱلْأَعْلَى with the elevation root ʿ-l-w; here YHWH is called ʿelyon, “Most High,” over all the earth, a related Semitic elevation title in a declaration of divine supremacy.

The commentary’s “Most High” language has a Hebrew counterpart in Melchizedek’s blessing of God as ʿelyon; the verse blesses that God for delivering Abram’s enemies, joining the title to praise and sovereignty.

The commentary sets the Lord’s highness against the low, near life and a ruler’s vaunted height; Isaiah calls God the High and Lofty One who also dwells with the contrite and lowly, redefining true elevation.

column5: majestic name and glory above the heavens
column6: The commentary says the named one is lifted by the name; this prayer calls YHWH’s name majestic throughout the earth and places his glory above the heavens.
The commentary contrasts the truly exalted Lord with a creature claiming the highest rank; this hymn places YHWH above all nations and his glory above the heavens.
The commentary’s al-aʿla denotes real divine elevation, unlike Pharaoh’s self-assertion; this praise asks who is like the Lord, enthroned on high.
The commentary’s command to glorify the Lord’s name is matched by Moses’ song, which calls the Lord “my God” and says he will praise and exalt him after the sea deliverance.

column5: exaltation and praise of the name
column6: The commentary links tasbih with raising the Lord’s name; Isaiah says “I will exalt you” and praise the Lord’s name for faithful wonders, giving that pairing a worship context.
The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of every fault; this psalm calls for praise of the Lord’s great, awesome name and declares him holy.
The commentary’s ذَكَرَ is “remembered/mentioned”; the psalmist says he remembered the Lord’s name at night and kept the law, a direct Hebrew cognate in a devotional setting.

The commentary links remembrance to the Lord’s name; God identifies himself to Moses and says this name is his memorial through all generations, using the Hebrew z-k-r family for enduring remembrance.

column5: remembering the Lord’s name against worldly reliance
column6: The commentary’s remembered name marks the worshipper’s orientation toward the Lord; this verse contrasts those who trust chariots and horses with those who remember the name of YHWH their God.

column5: remembrance and reverence for the name
column6: The commentary’s dhikr links remembrance with the Lord’s honor; Malachi says those who fear the Lord and esteem his name speak together, and a book of remembrance is written for them.

column5: remembered royal name and enduring praise
column6: The commentary says naming raises the named one’s remembrance; in this royal wedding poem the speaker promises the king’s name will be remembered through generations and peoples will praise him, though the addressee is the king, not explicitly YHWH.
The commentary cites houses raised for worship where the Lord’s name is mentioned; Solomon calls the temple the place where God said his name would be, tying a worship house to the indwelling name.

column5: a tower reaching heaven and a self-made name
column6: The commentary contrasts the Lord’s high name with a ruler’s false elevation; Babel’s builders seek a name for themselves while building a tower toward heaven, joining self-exaltation and name-making in one scene.

The commentary’s high/low axis includes a creature’s attempt to rise; after Babel’s tower project, God scatters the builders and the city is left unfinished, a narrative reversal of their ascent and self-made name.

column5: “I will make myself like the Most High”
column6: The commentary cites Pharaoh claiming “I am your Lord Most High”; the taunting king in Isaiah explicitly resolves to make himself like the Most High, exposing the same creaturely seizure of divine height.
The commentary says a king’s rising can mean tyranny and arrogance; Isaiah’s self-exalting figure is brought down to Sheol, supplying the reversal implicit in the Qur’anic judgment on Pharaoh.

The commentary’s Pharaoh appropriates the Lord’s highest title; Ezekiel addresses Tyre’s ruler as a man who says “I am a god” while sitting in a godlike seat, another ruler’s false claim to divine rank.

column5: king boasts of his own majesty
column6: The commentary identifies Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as arrogant self-exaltation; Nebuchadnezzar claims Babylon was built by his own power for the glory of his majesty, making the ruler’s boast explicit.

column5: Aramaic title for the Most High
column6: The commentary labels ٱلْأَعْلَى with an elevation root; after his humiliation Nebuchadnezzar blesses the Aramaic “Most High” and praises his everlasting dominion, coupling a related Semitic title with worship.
The commentary opposes God’s true highness to a creature’s arrogance; Nebuchadnezzar honors the King of heaven and concludes that those who walk in pride God is able to humble.

column5: human pride lowered, Lord alone exalted
column6: The commentary makes height reversible when a ruler exalts himself; Isaiah says the proud eyes of humanity will be brought low and YHWH alone exalted.

The commentary quotes Pharaoh’s direct claim to be the highest lord; Exodus instead has Pharaoh deny knowing YHWH and refuse obedience, preserving a distinct biblical portrayal of the same ruler’s resistance.

The commentary’s Pharaoh claims the highest rank for himself; God tells the biblical Pharaoh he has been kept standing so divine power may be shown and God’s name proclaimed throughout the earth, reversing the claim.

column5: magicians recognize God’s act but are not converted
column6: The commentary notes that Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Exodus has Pharaoh’s magicians admit “the finger of God” but remain in the confrontation, without the conversion and reward narrated in the Qur’anic scene.
The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of evil and cites divine majesty; Moses’ song asks who is like the Lord, majestic in holiness and awesome in deeds.

The commentary treats Pharaoh’s self-ascribed height as arrogance; Moses warns Israel against saying “my power and the might of my hand” made its wealth, a specific warning against taking divine provision as one’s own greatness.

column5: worship under threat of the furnace
column6: The commentary joins praise of the Lord’s high name to the great fire; after the three Judeans survive Nebuchadnezzar’s blazing furnace, the king blesses their God because they refused to worship any god but him.
The commentary names the great fire awaiting the wretched; Isaiah’s closing vision shows the corpses of rebels with an unquenched fire, a related scriptural image of divine judgment by fire.

The commentary labels سَبِّحِ as tasbih, glorifying God; Daniel thanks and praises the God of his fathers for revealing the king’s secret, using the Aramaic praise cognate in a prayer that credits divine wisdom.

column5: this world as a vestibule to the world to come
column6: The commentary hears al-dunya as the lower and nearer life that people choose; Avot calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation for entry into the latter.

column5: relative worth of the two worlds
column6: The commentary’s choice of the nearer life is a value judgment; Avot says one hour of good deeds in this world is better than the whole world to come, yet one hour of serenity in the world to come is better than all this world, preserving both sides of the contrast.

column5: magnifying and sanctifying the great name
column6: The commentary commands praise of the Lord’s high name; the Qaddish opens with a prayer that God’s great name be magnified and sanctified in the world he created.

column5: Babel’s tower as rebellion against God
column6: The commentary treats a creature’s claim to height as arrogant usurpation; Genesis Rabbah reads the tower builders’ ascent as rebellion against heaven, making the biblical tower more than an architectural project.

column5: worship and glorification of the Lord of Spirits’ name
column6: The commentary joins the Lord’s name to praise and highness; 1 Enoch pictures earth’s inhabitants falling down to worship and bless, glorify, and celebrate the name of the Lord of Spirits.

column5: prayer that the Father’s name be hallowed
column6: The commentary’s opening command is praise of the Lord’s name; Jesus’ prayer begins by asking that the Father’s name be hallowed, placing sanctification of the name inside communal prayer.
The commentary links the Lord’s name and remembered honor to elevation; Mary’s prayer begins by magnifying the Lord, a direct worship formula from a lowly speaker.
The commentary’s tasbih declares God free of defect and exalts his name; Mary says the Mighty One has done great things for her and holy is his name.
The commentary pairs a self-exalting ruler with the low/near life; Mary’s hymn says God brings rulers down from thrones and exalts the lowly, a direct reversal of claimed human height.
The commentary’s command to raise the Lord’s name is echoed when Jesus prays that the Father glorify his name; the heavenly voice answers that it has been glorified and will be glorified again.

column5: exalted and given the name above every name
column6: The commentary says the Lord’s name is raised and honored; Paul says God highly exalted Jesus and bestowed the name above every name, locating exaltation in the Christ hymn.

column5: every knee bows at the name
column6: The commentary’s name-and-prayer pairing becomes embodied worship here: at Jesus’ name every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth is to bow.
The commentary joins remembering the Lord’s name to prayer; Paul says every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord to the glory of God the Father.

column5: praise and confession of the name
column6: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord’s name before prayer; Hebrews describes continual praise as a sacrifice of lips that confess God’s name.
The commentary links tasbih, majesty, and the Lord’s name; Revelation asks who will not fear and glorify God’s name, then says he alone is holy and nations will worship.

column5: thanksgiving for the holy name in prayer
column6: The commentary’s remembered and praised name is a liturgical act; the post-meal prayer thanks the holy Father for his holy name made to dwell in believers’ hearts.
The commentary calls Pharaoh’s highest-lord claim arrogance; Jesus says the one who exalts himself will be humbled and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.

column5: humility before the Lord brings exaltation
column6: The commentary makes height and lowliness an axis; James commands readers to humble themselves before the Lord, who will exalt them.
The commentary contrasts the proud ruler with the lowly life; Peter tells believers to humble themselves under God’s mighty hand so he may exalt them at the proper time.
The commentary places Moses’ story beside the warning against choosing the near life; Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God’s people over the temporary pleasure of sin.

column5: Moses values reward above Egypt’s wealth
column6: The commentary’s low-life choice is a question of value; Hebrews says Moses considered reproach greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures because he looked to the reward.

column5: the world passes, God’s will abides
column6: The commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life; John contrasts the passing world and its desires with the one who does God’s will and abides forever.

column5: gaining the world and losing one’s life
column6: The commentary criticizes preferring the low, near life; Jesus asks what it profits someone to gain the whole world and forfeit life, making the choice’s cost explicit.

The commentary says Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Paul names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses who resist the truth, preserving a contrary Christian memory of the magicians.
The commentary links divine majesty and light with the great fire; Paul describes God as dwelling in unapproachable light and as the one to whom honor and eternal dominion belong.
The commentary names the great fire as the wretched person’s end; Jesus’ judgment scene sends the accursed into eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.
The commentary says people prefer the near, lower life; Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth, where moth and rust destroy, giving the choice a concrete object and cost.
Against the commentary’s preference for the near life, Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven, where it cannot be destroyed, supplying the alternative value.
